indications.text: Mainstay (first-line) therapy for acute otitis media. The higher dose is what overcomes Streptococcus pneumoniae resistance.
indications.edu: Given by mouth twice daily. The best duration is not established: 5–7 days, possibly up to 10, and 5 days may be too short for severe disease.
verify: S. pneumoniae resistance overcome with higher doses
5 days may be insufficient for severe disease

indications.text: Severe or resistant acute otitis media, or when the child received antibiotics in the previous month.
indications.edu: A step up from plain amoxicillin, not the first choice: keep it for severe or resistant disease or recent antibiotic exposure.
verify: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) for severe or resistant disease
previous antibiotics received in previous month

indications.drug:
Cefdinir or azithromycin
Omnicef; Zithromax (a macrolide)
indications.text: Acute otitis media in penicillin-allergic patients.
indications.edu: Up to 50% of Streptococcus pneumoniae is resistant to macrolides, so azithromycin is the less reliable of the two alternatives.
verify: Cefdinir (Omnicef) or azithromycin (Zithromax) for penicillin allergic patients

indications.drug:
Failed therapy
no improvement in 3 days
indications.text: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) or a third-generation cephalosporin (cefdinir, Omnicef) if no antibiotics were taken in the past 3 months.
indications.edu: Failed therapy is defined as no improvement in 3 days: switch drugs rather than repeat the same one.
verify: If no antibiotics in past 3 months

indications.text: Escalation for failed therapy, or when oral medications are not tolerated.
indications.edu: Given intramuscularly or intravenously; the intramuscular course is three doses, one every 24 hours.

indications.text: Standard therapy for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, because Haemophilus influenzae is often a beta-lactamase producer. The bacteria are the same as in otitis media, plus Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus and gram-negative bacilli.
indications.edu: Call it bacterial only if symptoms last more than 10 days or worsen at about day 5–6; otherwise presume a virus. Duration: children 10–14 days, adults 5–7 days. Saline irrigations can be useful for congestion: use only distilled, sterile or previously boiled water, never straight tap water (rare but deadly amoeba infection of the brain).
verify: high instance of beta lactamase producing H. influenzae

indications.drug:
Penicillin-allergy regimens
clindamycin (Cleocin) plus cefixime (Suprax), or levofloxacin (Levaquin)
indications.text: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a penicillin-allergic patient.
indications.edu: Clindamycin is rough on the gut flora (risk of Clostridioides difficile diarrhea), and levofloxacin resistance varies by area, so check local resistance patterns.

indications.text: Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS) pharyngitis: once daily for 10 days. The goal is to prevent acute rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
indications.edu: Pharyngitis is mainly viral (group A strep is only 15–30% of cases), so use a rapid strep test to prevent over-prescribing.

indications.text: A single intramuscular injection for group A strep pharyngitis, as the alternative to a 10-day oral course of amoxicillin.
indications.edu: One injection replaces the full 10 days of oral treatment.

indications.text: Group A strep pharyngitis in a penicillin-allergic patient.
indications.edu: Used only when penicillin cannot be given.

indications.drug:
Otic antibiotic drops
ciprofloxacin, ofloxacin, combinations with a steroid
indications.text: Otitis media and otitis externa (and similar ear infections).
indications.edu: Check that the eardrum is intact before using drops: polymyxin B is not recommended with a ruptured eardrum or tubes in place.
verify: not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place

indications.drug:
Available otic agents
ciprofloxacin; ciprofloxacin/dexamethasone (Ciprodex); neomycin, polymyxin B, hydrocortisone (Cortisporin); ofloxacin
indications.text: Ear drops usually mix an anti-infective with a glucocorticoid.
indications.edu: The anti-infective inhibits bacterial growth; the steroid decreases production of inflammatory cytokines.

indications.text: Otic drops for otitis media and otitis externa.
indications.edu: Expensive. The alternative is ofloxacin plus ophthalmic dexamethasone drops.

indications.drug:
Neomycin, polymyxin B and hydrocortisone
Cortisporin
indications.text: Otic drops for otitis externa. Otitis media is listed for otic drops as a group, but when tubes are in place or the eardrum is ruptured this combination is the one to avoid.
indications.edu: Neomycin can cause hypersensitivity. Polymyxin B is not recommended with a ruptured eardrum or tubes in place (cochlear damage and hearing loss).

indications.text: Systemic fungal infections.
indications.edu: Taken systemically, so screen the medication list for interactions (it is a cytochrome P450 3A4 [CYP3A4] inhibitor).

indications.text: Oral candidiasis (thrush), which is seen with inhaled steroids, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) infection or AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) and chemotherapy.
indications.edu: It is not absorbed, so it acts only in the mouth and gut and causes little more than stomach upset.

indications.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
indications.text: The effect depends on exposure: antiplatelet at the lowest range, antipyretic-analgesic (fever and pain) at the next, and anti-inflammatory at the highest therapeutic range.
indications.edu: The same drug becomes toxic (salicylism) above the anti-inflammatory range. Bleeding is the complication at antiplatelet exposure and ringing in the ears (tinnitus) signals the anti-inflammatory range.

indications.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
indications.text: Over-the-counter self-treatment of fever and pain: take if fever is above 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
indications.edu: Follow up immediately if fever is not held below 102 degrees Fahrenheit on treatment, or stays above 100 for more than 3 days; follow up if pain worsens or lasts more than 10 days. Drink plenty of fluids. Do not combine with other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or with anticoagulants (aspirin inhibits platelet function).
verify: Do not take aspirin and other NSAIDS
Do not take if taking anticoagulants

indications.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
indications.text: Relief of mild to moderate pain. A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic.
indications.edu: It reversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase 1 and 2 (unlike aspirin). Taken by mouth three to four times daily as needed for pain.
verify: Indications: relief mild to moderate pain

indications.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
indications.text: Another over-the-counter nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) alongside ibuprofen.
indications.edu: Longer half-life, so it is dosed less often than ibuprofen.

indications.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
indications.text: Pain and fever above 100 degrees Fahrenheit. An analgesic and antipyretic.
indications.edu: Very well tolerated at therapeutic doses, but the daily maximum is 4 grams in 24 hours — the one dose worth knowing (lower it, or avoid the drug, with existing liver disease). Count every acetaminophen-containing product toward it, including combination cold remedies and prescription pain tablets. Taken every 4–6 hours as needed for fever.
verify: no notable side effects at therapeutic doses

indications.text: Allergic reactions (allergic rhinitis, urticaria, insect bites, drug hypersensitivity); motion sickness, nausea and vestibular disturbances; over-the-counter sleep remedies; and an adjuvant role in anaphylaxis.
indications.edu: In anaphylaxis they are an add-on only, never the main treatment.
verify: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, insect bites, drug hypersensitivity
Motion Sickness, nausea and vestibular disturbances

indications.drug:
First versus second generation
doxylamine (sleep aid) vs second generation
indications.text: First-generation agents are available over the counter as sleep aids (doxylamine).
indications.edu: Second-generation agents cause much less sedation because they cross into the central nervous system poorly: choose them when the patient needs to stay alert (for example, someone who drives for work).

indications.text: Motion sickness: it has the strongest antimuscarinic actions among the H1 antagonists.
indications.edu: Its antiemetic action involves the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) in the brain; antimuscarinic actions also decrease nasal and bronchial secretions during allergic rhinitis.

indications.text: Allergic rhinitis and vasomotor rhinitis.
indications.edu: An intranasal H1 antagonist, sprayed into each nostril twice daily.

indications.text: How to use an intranasal spray correctly.
indications.edu: Blow the nose and clear the nostrils, tilt the head down, and angle the spray away from the septum (right hand for the left nostril, left hand for the right). Do not tilt the head back (it draws the drug into the throat). Clean the tip with a tissue and do not use with other nasal sprays. If a nosebleed develops, stop and follow up immediately; follow up if symptoms worsen or do not improve.
verify: Do not use with other nasal sprays

indications.drug:
Nasal corticosteroid names
beclomethasone (Beconase AQ), budesonide (Rhinocort, over-the-counter), flunisolide (Nasalide), fluticasone (Flonase, over-the-counter), mometasone (Nasonex), triamcinolone (Nasacort)
indications.text: The six nasal corticosteroids to recognize by name.
indications.edu: Many have inhaled versions for asthma: do not mix up the names. Fluticasone (Flonase) is the nasal product, not Flovent.
verify: don’t get the names mixed up

indications.text: Allergic rhinitis and vasomotor rhinitis.
indications.edu: No interaction information is available. Side effects are mostly local at usual doses (nosebleed, septal perforation, unpleasant taste).

indications.text: Allergic rhinitis and drug hypersensitivity reactions.
indications.edu: A systemic steroid with many adverse effects; it weakens the immune system (decreased resistance to infections).

indications.text: Counseling for a systemic corticosteroid course.
indications.edu: Do not discontinue abruptly if taken for more than 1 week. It weakens your immune system.

indications.text: Allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis and drug hypersensitivity reactions.
indications.edu: Prednisone is the tablet; prednisolone (Orapred) is the liquid formulation.

indications.text: Counseling for a systemic corticosteroid course.
indications.edu: Do not discontinue abruptly (rebound symptoms). The patient is considered immunocompromised: avoid exposure to chickenpox and measles, and avoid live vaccines; it weakens the immune system.

indications.text: Nasal congestion. An alpha agonist that constricts the blood vessels of the nasal lining.
indications.edu: Maximum 3–5 days. Longer use causes rebound rhinitis (rhinitis medicamentosa). Used twice daily.

indications.text: How to use the nasal spray safely.
indications.edu: Do not use for more than 3–5 days. Blow the nose and clear the nostrils, tilt the head toward the toes, angle the spray away from the septum (right hand for the left nostril, left hand for the right), and do not tilt the head back. If a nosebleed develops, stop and follow up immediately. Do not use with other nasal sprays.
verify: Do not use more than 3-5 days

indications.text: Nasal congestion from the common cold, hay fever or allergies; sinus congestion; eustachian tube dysfunction from a viral infection.
indications.edu: An oral alpha agonist, so it acts on blood vessels throughout the body; it may weaken the effect of blood pressure medicines.
verify: Relieves nasal congestion due to common cold, hay fever or allergies
Eustachian tube dysfunction due to viral infection

indications.text: Symptomatic relief of non-productive cough. An antitussive that anesthetizes the stretch receptors in the lungs.
indications.edu: Swallow whole: do not chew, cut or crush (chewing causes local anesthesia of the mouth). Taken as needed for cough, up to three times daily.

indications.text: Cough. An antitussive related to codeine that suppresses the cough center in the medulla.
indications.edu: Check for a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) taken now or within 2 weeks, and for other drugs that raise serotonin (risk of serotonin syndrome).
verify: within 2 weeks of taking an MAOI

indications.text: Loosens mucus and decreases its viscosity.
indications.edu: No interaction information is available; nausea and vomiting are possible.

indications.text: Counseling for a mucus-loosening medicine.
indications.edu: Drink plenty of fluid and expect an increase in drainage. Follow up if symptoms persist for more than 7 days or worsen.
verify: more than 7 days or worsen f/u

indications.text: Cystic fibrosis (CF): it reduces the viscosity of CF sputum, improves lung function and decreases exacerbations in mild to moderate lung disease.
indications.edu: A DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) enzyme that cleaves DNA from degenerating neutrophils; nebulized once daily. It is also effective in severe disease, but lung function improves less.
verify: Reduces the viscosity of CF sputum

indications.text: Loosens airway mucus: reported to improve mucus flow properties, mucus transport, airway hydration, mucociliary clearance and lung function.
indications.edu: Inhaled twice daily as a 7% (hypertonic) solution.

indications.text: Traditional treatment for acetaminophen toxicity. When inhaled (nebulized) it is a mucolytic that reduces mucus viscosity.
indications.edu: It splits the disulfide bonds linking mucoproteins; inhaled use smells of rotten eggs (high sulfur content).

sideeffects.text: Chance of hypersensitivity (allergic reaction).
sideeffects.monitor: Watch for new itching or worsening inflammation of the ear after starting the drops.

sideeffects.text: Cochlear damage and hearing loss when the drops reach the inner ear through a ruptured eardrum or tubes.
sideeffects.monitor: Examine the eardrum before every use; do not use with a perforation or tubes in place.
verify: not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place

sideeffects.text: QTc (corrected QT interval) prolongation. Hepatitis, abnormal liver function tests, cirrhosis and hepatic failure. Hyperlipidemia and orthostatic hypotension. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitor, so it raises levels of drugs cleared by that enzyme. Also an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning for oral ketoconazole: liver injury, and QT prolongation with interacting drugs.
sideeffects.monitor: Review every other medication for CYP3A4 interactions; monitor the electrocardiogram (QTc), liver function tests and lipids, and watch for dizziness on standing.
verify: Hepatitis, abnormal LFT, cirrhosis, hepatic failure

sideeffects.text: Diarrhea, nausea, stomach pain and vomiting.
sideeffects.monitor: Little to monitor: it is a nonabsorbable antifungal, so effects stay in the gut.

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.text: Bleeding (antiplatelet range); bleeding, gastrointestinal upset, nausea and hypersensitivity (fever and pain range); tinnitus (anti-inflammatory range).
sideeffects.monitor: Ringing in the ears is the audible marker that exposure has climbed into the anti-inflammatory range; watch for bruising, black stools and stomach pain.

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.text: Salicylism: hyperventilation and alkalosis; then fever, dehydration and metabolic acidosis; then shock, coma, respiratory and renal failure, and death.
sideeffects.monitor: Treat any suspected overdose as an emergency; hyperventilation and ringing in the ears are early warnings.
verify: Shock, coma, respiratory and renal failure, death

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.drug:
Aspirin — Reye syndrome
fatty liver encephalopathy
sideeffects.text: Reye syndrome: vomiting, progressive central nervous system damage, hepatic injury and hypoglycemia. Fatty change of the liver and kidney tubules, cerebral edema and mitochondrial dysfunction. Children under 15; mortality 50%.
sideeffects.monitor: Occurs after an upper respiratory infection, influenza or chickenpox: never give aspirin to a child with a fever from a viral illness; vomiting and a change in behavior after aspirin need urgent evaluation.

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.drug: Aspirin — the five stages of Reye syndrome
sideeffects.text: I rash on hands and feet, vomiting, high fever, lethargy; II encephalitis, hyperventilation, fatty liver; III coma, cerebral edema; IV deeper coma, fixed dilated pupils, hepatic dysfunction; V seizures, multiple organ failure, death.
sideeffects.monitor: The early stage looks like the viral illness it follows, so vomiting plus lethargy in a child who took aspirin is the trigger to act.
verify: rash on hands & feet, vomiting, high fever, lethargy

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.text: Gastric or duodenal ulcers, perforation and bleeding. Edema and fluid retention. Acute renal failure and decreased creatinine clearance. Prescription nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs also carry an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning for cardiovascular events and gastrointestinal bleeding.
sideeffects.monitor: Monitor kidney function (creatinine clearance) and watch for signs of stomach bleeding and swelling; risk climbs with regular daily use.

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.text: No notable side effects at therapeutic doses; very well tolerated.
sideeffects.monitor: Stay within the fixed daily maximum, counting every product that contains it; too much damages the liver.
verify: no notable side effects at therapeutic doses

sideeffects.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
sideeffects.text: Alcohol plus acetaminophen increases the risk of liver damage (chronically).
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about regular alcohol use and pre-existing liver disease before recommending it.

sideeffects.text: Sedation is the major side effect and is additive with other central nervous system depressants or alcohol. Restlessness and excitation at higher doses (especially in children); excitation is seen in overdose.
sideeffects.monitor: Warn about driving and alcohol. Second-generation agents cause much less sedation.
verify: Additive with other CNS depressants or alcohol
Restlessness and excitation at higher doses

sideeffects.drug: First-generation H1 antagonists — class adverse effects
sideeffects.text: Sedation; gastrointestinal disturbances; antimuscarinic effects: dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision; with topical use, hypersensitivity (dermatitis, photosensitivity).
sideeffects.monitor: Ask about difficulty urinating and vision change; advise sun protection with topical use.
verify: dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision

sideeffects.text: Bitter taste and epistaxis (nosebleed).
sideeffects.monitor: If a nosebleed develops, stop the spray and follow up.

sideeffects.drug:
Nasal corticosteroids
beclomethasone, budesonide, flunisolide, fluticasone, mometasone, triamcinolone
sideeffects.text: Epistaxis (nosebleed), septal perforation and an unpleasant taste.
sideeffects.monitor: Effects are mostly local at usual doses; check the septum if nosebleeds recur.

sideeffects.text: Congestive heart failure, hypertension and fluid retention; glucose intolerance; hirsutism, cushingoid features, potassium loss, sodium retention, tendon rupture; papilledema, glaucoma, increased intraocular pressure, cataracts, exophthalmos; decreased resistance to infections.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch blood pressure, weight and swelling, glucose, potassium, eye pressure and signs of infection; time and dose drive the risk, so keep courses short.
verify: Hirsutism, cushingoid, potassium loss, sodium retention, tendon rupture
Papilledema, glaucoma, increased IOP, cataracts, exophthalmos

sideeffects.text: Sodium and fluid retention, congestive heart failure, hypertension, low potassium; tendon rupture and pathologic fractures of long bones; increased liver function tests, cushingoid features, glucose intolerance; cataracts, increased intraocular pressure, glaucoma, exophthalmos; compromised immune system.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch blood pressure, fluid status, potassium, glucose, liver function tests, eye pressure and signs of infection.
verify: Sodium retention, fluid retention, CHF, HTN, low potassium
Tendon rupture, pathologic fractures of long bones

sideeffects.text: Rebound rhinitis (rhinitis medicamentosa) if used for more than 3–5 days. Hypertension.
sideeffects.monitor: Count the days of use; a patient stuck in rebound needs to taper off, not simply reuse the spray.

sideeffects.text: Tachycardia, hypertension and headache. Decreases the effect of blood pressure medicines.
sideeffects.monitor: Check blood pressure and heart rate; ask about antihypertensive use.

sideeffects.text: Local anesthesia of the mouth from chewing the capsule.
sideeffects.monitor: Ensure the capsule is swallowed whole.
verify: local anesthesia from chewing the capsule

sideeffects.text: Confusion, excitement and agitation. Risk for serotonin syndrome with other pro-serotonergic drugs.
sideeffects.monitor: Review the medication list for antidepressants and other serotonin-raising drugs.

sideeffects.text: Nausea and vomiting.
sideeffects.monitor: No interaction information is available.

sideeffects.text: Rotten-egg smell (high sulfur content), nausea and vomiting, and bronchospasm with the inhaled route.
sideeffects.monitor: Watch the breathing of any patient who wheezes, especially after nebulization.

contra.text: Chance of hypersensitivity: stop if itching or inflammation worsens.
Not recommended with a ruptured eardrum (tympanic membrane) or tubes in place: the drug can reach the cochlea and cause damage and hearing loss. Choose a different drop in that patient.
verify: not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place

contra.text: Cautions: QTc (corrected QT interval) prolongation, hepatic toxicity (hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatic failure) and cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibition, which raises levels of drugs cleared by that enzyme.
verify: Hepatitis, abnormal LFT, cirrhosis, hepatic failure

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Salicylism: the toxic syndrome of hyperventilation, alkalosis, metabolic acidosis, shock, coma and renal and respiratory failure at high exposure.

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Contraindicated in bleeding disorders (irreversible platelet inhibition).

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Contraindicated in pregnancy, although very low doses may be of benefit in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (preeclampsia).

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Contraindicated in children with fever associated with viral disease (chickenpox, influenza): increased incidence of Reye syndrome.
verify: Children with fever associated with viral disease

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.drug:
Aspirin — Reye syndrome
fatty liver encephalopathy
contra.text: Reye syndrome: children under 15, mortality 50%; vomiting, progressive central nervous system damage, liver injury and hypoglycemia after an upper respiratory infection, influenza or chickenpox.

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Do not combine with anticoagulants (aspirin inhibits platelet function) or with other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
verify: Do not take aspirin and other NSAIDS
Do not take if taking anticoagulants

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Allergy to the product is a contraindication; avoid with a past history of stomach ulcers or perforation, or with renal dysfunction (listed as relative or absolute).
verify: PMHx of stomach ulcers/perforation, renal dysfunction

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: May exacerbate asthma.

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Avoid in children younger than 6 months.
verify: Avoid in children < 6 months of age

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Decreases the effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors; with diuretics watch for renal failure; decreases lithium excretion (levels rise); decreases methotrexate excretion (toxic levels); increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants (serious gastrointestinal bleeds).

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Contraindicated in allergy to the product (the only listed contraindication).

contra.group: Aspirin, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen
contra.text: Alcohol increases the risk of liver damage (chronically).
verify: Alcohol & Tylenol can increase risk of liver damage

contra.text: Additive sedation with other central nervous system depressants or alcohol; excitation instead of sedation at higher doses, especially in children, and in overdose.
verify: Additive with other CNS depressants or alcohol
Restlessness and excitation at higher doses (especially children)

contra.text: Stop and follow up immediately if a nosebleed develops. Do not use with other nasal sprays.
verify: If nosebleed develops, d/c Rx & f/u immediately
Do not use with other nasal sprays

contra.text: With a diuretic, hypokalemia; with digoxin, increased risk of arrhythmia because of hypokalemia; macrolides decrease its clearance; it decreases the effect of antidiabetic drugs.
verify: increased risk of arrhythmia due to hypokalemia

contra.text: Contraindicated in systemic fungal infections.
Do not discontinue abruptly if taken for more than 1 week.
Contraindicated in allergy to the product; avoid in infections, especially fungal ones (listed as relative or absolute), because the steroid weakens immunity.
Do not discontinue abruptly: rebound symptoms.
Avoid exposure to chickenpox and measles, and avoid live vaccines: the patient is considered immunocompromised.
Rhinitis medicamentosa: rebound congestion when used for more than 3–5 days.
Interacts with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and antidepressants. Do not use for more than 3–5 days.
verify: Do not use more than 3-5 days

contra.text: Decreases the effect of antihypertensives, and causes tachycardia and hypertension.
Contraindicated in allergy to the product or related products (tetracaine).
verify: Allergic to product or related products (tetracaine)

contra.text: Contraindicated if taking, or within 2 weeks of taking, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).
verify: currently taking or within 2 weeks of taking an MAOI

contra.text: Serotonin syndrome risk with other pro-serotonergic drugs.
Contraindicated in allergy to the product.
Bronchospasm is a listed adverse reaction of the inhaled route: use with care in patients with airway disease.

killers.what: Children under 15, mortality 50%: vomiting, progressive central nervous system damage, liver injury and hypoglycemia after influenza, chickenpox or an upper respiratory infection. Never give aspirin to a child with a viral fever; warn parents in advance. Stop and evaluate urgently.

Hyperventilation and alkalosis, then fever, dehydration and metabolic acidosis, then shock, coma, respiratory and renal failure and death. Ringing in the ears (tinnitus) is the early warning that exposure is too high.
verify: Shock, coma, respiratory and renal failure, death

killers.what: A life-threatening arrhythmia risk, made worse by any other QT-prolonging or cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) interacting drug. Check the electrocardiogram and the medication list.
Liver injury from a systemic antifungal. Stop the drug and evaluate the liver if liver function tests rise.
verify: Hepatitis, abnormal LFT, cirrhosis, hepatic failure

killers.what: Permanent inner-ear injury when the drops pass a ruptured eardrum or tubes. Examine the eardrum first; do not use polymyxin B if it is perforated or tubes are in place.
verify: not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place

killers.effect: Gastric or duodenal ulcer, perforation and bleeding
killers.what: Bleeding ulcers and perforation, mainly with regular daily use. Warn patients about black stools and stomach pain; stop and evaluate.
Decreased creatinine clearance and acute renal failure; worst in patients who already have kidney disease or take diuretics. Stop and check kidney function.
Chronic alcohol use increases the risk of liver damage; a fixed daily maximum applies and every acetaminophen-containing product counts toward it. Warn the patient in advance.

killers.drugs: dexamethasone with digoxin or a diuretic
killers.what: Potassium loss from the steroid, worsened by a diuretic, raises the arrhythmia risk with digoxin. Monitor potassium and the electrocardiogram.
verify: increased risk of arrhythmia due to hypokalemia

killers.what: Risk with other pro-serotonergic drugs, and the drug is contraindicated with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) taken now or within 2 weeks. Stop and evaluate agitation, confusion or fever.
verify: within 2 weeks of taking an MAOI

killers.what: Airway narrowing with the nebulized route. Stop and treat wheezing or breathlessness.

commons.what: The major side effect of the whole class and additive with alcohol and other depressants; second-generation agents cause much less. It is why doxylamine works as a sleep aid.
verify: Additive with other CNS depressants or alcohol

commons.effect: Dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision
commons.what: The antimuscarinic set, plus gastrointestinal disturbances; with topical use, dermatitis and photosensitivity.
verify: dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision

commons.effect: Gastric and duodenal ulcer, edema and renal effects
commons.what: Stomach, fluid and kidney effects are the class pattern for these drugs.

commons.effect: Fluid retention, hypertension, potassium loss, glucose intolerance
commons.what: Salt and water retention, raised blood pressure, low potassium and high glucose belong to the class, not the individual drug.

commons.effect: Cataracts, glaucoma, increased intraocular pressure, infection risk
commons.what: Eye effects and weakened immunity are shared by the class; risk rises with dose and duration.

Mostly local effects at usual doses. The source gives no interaction information (that is not the same as no interactions); strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole can raise systemic exposure to some nasal steroids.
Vasoconstriction spreads beyond the nose, and the oral agent also weakens antihypertensive treatment.

commons.effect: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and stomach pain
commons.what: Expected, minor gastrointestinal upset; not a reason to stop.

zebras.what: Use beyond 3–5 days causes rebound congestion, and patients reuse the spray to treat it. Limit to 3–5 days.
Ringing in the ears appears in the anti-inflammatory exposure range, before frank toxicity.
Raises levels of many drugs cleared by CYP3A4, so it interacts with many medicines.
The component most likely to cause an allergic reaction in otic drops.

zebras.effect: Numbing of the mouth when the capsule is chewed
zebras.what: Local anesthesia from chewing; hence swallow whole. Cross-allergy is possible with related local anesthetics such as tetracaine.
verify: local anesthesia from chewing the capsule

zebras.what: The high sulfur content gives inhaled N-acetylcysteine a rotten-egg smell, alongside nausea and vomiting.
The bitter taste is listed alongside nosebleed for this nasal spray.
The central nervous system effects listed for this antitussive.
Listed among dexamethasone's adverse effects, but not unique to it: prednisone and prednisolone share the same steroid side effects, so treat these as class effects.

zebras.effect: Pathologic fractures of long bones and raised liver enzymes
zebras.what: Listed among prednisone's adverse effects, but not unique to it: dexamethasone and other glucocorticoids share the same bone and steroid effects, so treat these as class effects.

chart.title: ENT drug chart: which drug for which problem
chart.sub: Antibiotics, ear drops, antifungals, pain and fever relievers, antihistamines, steroids, decongestants and cough agents on one page.

cells:
Amoxicillin, high dose
Amoxil — acute otitis media
Acute otitis media, first line (mainstay of therapy)
Higher dose overcomes Streptococcus pneumoniae resistance; step up to amoxicillin-clavulanate for severe or resistant disease or recent antibiotics
Treat 5–7 days, possibly up to 10; 5 days may be too short for severe disease
verify: S. pneumoniae resistance overcome with higher doses
Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) for severe or resistant disease
5 days may be insufficient for severe disease
rows.title: Ear, nose and throat (ENT) drug chart: which drug for which problem

cells: Up to 50% of Streptococcus pneumoniae is resistant to macrolides (azithromycin)
Complete the course (5–7 days, possibly up to 10)
verify: Cefdinir (Omnicef) or azithromycin (Zithromax) for penicillin allergic patients

cells: Failed therapy (no improvement in 3 days) or oral drugs not tolerated
Intramuscular or intravenous drug; the intramuscular course needs three visits or injections
Three intramuscular doses, one every 24 hours
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, standard therapy (beta-lactamase producing Haemophilus influenzae); penicillin allergy: clindamycin plus cefixime, or levofloxacin
Only call it bacterial after more than 10 days of symptoms or worsening at day 5–6
Children 10–14 days, adults 5–7 days; saline irrigations can help (use distilled or sterile water)

Amoxicillin or benzathine penicillin G
pharyngitis; allergy: cephalexin, clindamycin, azithromycin
Group A strep pharyngitis: amoxicillin for 10 days, or one intramuscular benzathine penicillin G injection

Mostly viral (group A strep 15–30%): use a rapid strep test to avoid over-prescribing; a positive test confirms treatment, but a negative rapid test still needs a backup culture because false negatives occur; goal is to prevent acute rheumatic fever
Finish the 10 days of amoxicillin, or accept a single injection

Neomycin, polymyxin B, hydrocortisone
Cortisporin ear drops
Otitis externa (otitis media is listed for otic drops as a group, but avoid this combination with tubes or a ruptured eardrum)
Neomycin: hypersensitivity. Polymyxin B: not recommended with a ruptured eardrum or tubes in place (cochlear damage, hearing loss)
verify: not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place

cells: Otitis media and otitis externa (steroid plus antibiotic drops)
Cheaper alternative: ofloxacin drops plus ophthalmic dexamethasone
QTc (corrected QT interval) prolongation; hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatic failure; hyperlipidemia; orthostatic hypotension; cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) inhibitor
Review all other medicines for interactions
verify: Hepatitis, abnormal LFT, cirrhosis, hepatic failure

cells: Oral candidiasis (thrush): seen with inhaled steroids, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection or acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), and chemotherapy
Diarrhea, nausea, stomach pain, vomiting only
Not absorbed, so it treats the mouth and gut only
Antiplatelet (lowest range); antipyretic-analgesic; anti-inflammatory (highest therapeutic range)
Bleeding; gastrointestinal upset and nausea; tinnitus in the anti-inflammatory range; then salicylism (hyperventilation, alkalosis, metabolic acidosis, shock, coma, death)
Ringing in the ears is the warning that exposure is too high

ASPIRIN — REYE SYNDROME
never for a child with a viral fever
Contraindicated: bleeding disorders, pregnancy, and children with fever from viral disease (chickenpox, influenza)
REYE SYNDROME: increased incidence in children with viral fever
Do not give aspirin to a child with chickenpox, influenza or another viral fever
verify: Children with fever associated with viral disease

cells: Follows aspirin given during an upper respiratory infection, influenza or chickenpox
Children under 15; mortality 50%: vomiting, progressive central nervous system damage, hepatic injury, hypoglycemia
Vomiting with lethargy after a viral illness treated with aspirin needs urgent evaluation
verify: Upper respiratory infection, Influenza or Chicken Pox

cells: Over-the-counter fever and pain: take if fever is above 100 degrees Fahrenheit
Do not take with anticoagulants (platelet inhibition); do not combine with other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Follow up if fever is not held below 102 or stays above 100 for more than 3 days; follow up if pain worsens or lasts more than 10 days; drink plenty of fluids
verify: Do not take aspirin and other NSAIDS
Do not take if taking anticoagulants

cells: Gastric or duodenal ulcers, perforation, bleeding; edema and fluid retention; acute renal failure
Taken by mouth three to four times daily as needed for pain
verify: Indications: relief mild to moderate pain

cells: Longer half-life, so it is dosed less often
Pain and fever above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (analgesic and antipyretic)
No notable side effects at therapeutic doses, but a fixed daily maximum applies: liver damage when exceeded
Count every product that contains acetaminophen toward the daily maximum
verify: no notable side effects at therapeutic doses

cells: Alcohol plus acetaminophen increases the risk of liver damage (chronically); allergy is the only contraindication
Ask about regular alcohol use and liver disease
Allergic reactions (rhinitis, urticaria, insect bites, drug hypersensitivity); motion sickness, nausea, vestibular disturbances; sleep remedies
Sedation and antimuscarinic effects with first-generation agents; only an adjuvant (add-on) in anaphylaxis
Over-the-counter sleep remedies are first-generation agents
verify: Motion Sickness, nausea and vestibular disturbances

cells: Sedation is the major side effect, additive with alcohol and other depressants; restlessness and excitation at higher doses, especially in children
verify: Additive with other CNS depressants or alcohol
Restlessness and excitation at higher doses

cells: Very sedating, with the strongest antimuscarinic actions of the group (dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision); additive with alcohol and other central nervous system depressants
Sprayed twice daily; stop and follow up if a nosebleed develops

Nasal spray technique
azelastine; the same steps apply to oxymetazoline
If a nosebleed develops, stop and follow up immediately; do not use with other nasal sprays
Blow the nose, tilt the head down, angle the spray away from the septum (right hand for the left nostril); do not tilt the head back; clean the tip
verify: Do not use with other nasal sprays

cells:
Nasal corticosteroids
beclomethasone, budesonide, flunisolide, fluticasone, mometasone, triamcinolone
Epistaxis, septal perforation, unpleasant taste (mostly local)

Nasal steroid names
Beconase AQ, Rhinocort, Nasalide, Flonase, Nasonex, Nasacort
Many have inhaled versions for asthma
Do not mix up nasal and inhaled products (Flonase is not Flovent)
verify: Many have inhaled versions for asthma

cells: Fluid retention, hypertension, glucose intolerance, potassium loss, tendon rupture, eye effects, decreased resistance to infections
verify: Papilledema, glaucoma, increased IOP, cataracts, exophthalmos

cells: Do not discontinue abruptly if taken for more than 1 week; it weakens your immune system
Allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, drug hypersensitivity reactions
Sodium and fluid retention, hypertension, low potassium, tendon rupture, pathologic fractures, cataracts, glaucoma, immune suppression
verify: Tendon rupture, pathologic fractures of long bones

cells: Allergy to the product; avoid in infections, especially fungal (relative or absolute)
Do not stop abruptly (rebound symptoms); immunocompromised: avoid exposure to chickenpox and measles, and avoid live vaccines
Rebound rhinitis (rhinitis medicamentosa) if used more than 3–5 days; hypertension
Do not use for more than 3–5 days
Nasal congestion from a cold, hay fever or allergies; sinus congestion; eustachian tube dysfunction from a viral infection
Tachycardia, hypertension, headache; decreased effect of antihypertensives
verify: Relieves nasal congestion due to common cold, hay fever or allergies
Eustachian tube dysfunction due to viral infection

cells: Local anesthesia of the mouth if the capsule is chewed; contraindicated in allergy to it or related products (tetracaine)
Swallow whole; do not chew, cut or crush
verify: local anesthesia from chewing the capsule

cells: Confusion, excitement, agitation; serotonin syndrome with other pro-serotonergic drugs; contraindicated with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) taken now or within 2 weeks
Review antidepressants and the MAOI washout period
verify: within 2 weeks of taking an MAOI

cells: Nausea and vomiting; allergy is the only contraindication
Drink plenty of fluid; expect an increase in drainage; follow up if symptoms last more than 7 days or worsen
verify: more than 7 days or worsen f/u

cells: Cystic fibrosis: reduces the viscosity of sputum, improves lung function, decreases exacerbations (mild to moderate disease)
verify: Reduces the viscosity of CF sputum

cells: Improves mucus flow, transport, airway hydration, mucociliary clearance and lung function
Traditional treatment for acetaminophen toxicity; mucolytic when inhaled
Expect a rotten-egg smell (high sulfur content); report wheezing after nebulization

chart.notes: Two warnings to know cold. Aspirin is never given to a child with a viral fever (chickenpox, influenza): Reye syndrome. Acetaminophen has a fixed daily maximum that counts every product containing it, and regular alcohol raises the risk of liver damage. A dash means the source does not state that item for the drug.

charts.title: Antihistamine Comparison
charts.sub: Every antihistamine on the slides side by side: how long it lasts, and how sedating, antiemetic and anticholinergic it is. First-generation agents are the sedating ones.
charts.notes: The pattern to know: the second-generation agents (cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine) are the least sedating and have almost no anticholinergic effect, and cetirizine and loratadine last 24 hours. First-generation agents are sedating and anticholinergic; promethazine and hydroxyzine are strongly antiemetic. This is the table behind the patient who drives for a living.

verify: Fexofenadine (Allegra) 12 Very low None Very low
Loratadine (Claritin) 24 Very low None Very low

charts.title: Histamine Receptor Actions
charts.sub: Where the H1 and H2 receptors are and what histamine does at each, the reason antihistamines do what they do.
charts.notes: H1 blockers (the antihistamines on the comparison chart) act on the H1 rows: itch and pain, swelling from leaky venules, bronchial contraction. The H2 receptors run gastric acid secretion, which is why H2 blockers treat acid, not allergy. The slide puts heart rate on H1 and force of contraction on H2; some references put both on H2. Know the slide’s version for this exam.

verify: Vascular H1 and H2 decreases TPR
Heart H2 increases force of contraction
GI mucosa H2 Gastric Acid and pepsin secretion
Cutaneous Nerve endings H1 Pain and itch
